For example, France, who reached the World Cup final in 2006, are down in 12th, while England, who failed even to qualify for Euro 2008, are ninth. Moreover, Les Bleus were at their lowest-ever position in the rankings in April 1998, when they stood 25th. Three months later, they lifted the World Cup.

From 2001 to 2006, Mexico were firmly established in the top 10, at one point rising as high as fourth, leaving many European fans wondering how that was possible. They were ranked ahead of a number of supposed European powerhouses, including Portugal. Not only did the Iberian nation reach the final of Euro 2004, but they also made the semi-finals of the World Cup in Germany two years later.

LONDON, England (CNN) — Spain have held on to first place in FIFA’s global rankings for the ninth month in a row, according to the latest list published by football’s world governing body.

The reigning European champions sit at No. 1 in FIFA’s standings. Spain have not been beaten since a 1-0 friendly defeat against Romania in Cadiz in November 2006. They also lead their qualifying group for the 2010 World Cup, having won all four of their matches, and have allowed just one goal in their past 10 international fixtures.

With a record like that, no other side can really match them, which is why Spain occupy the top position.

FIFA’s rankings are calculated using national-team results from the previous four years. More recent games and more important matches are given greater value, in an effort to show how strong a team is in the present competitive landscape.

Even so, supporters around the globe have often debated how meaningful the rankings really are.

Following the 2008 African Cup of Nations, American football writer Ives Galarcep commented: “Don’t try making any sense of these rankings. After all, Egypt, which just won the African Cup of Nations for a second straight time, is ranked 29th, fourth best among African teams.”

Do you believe FIFA’s rankings are worth much? Share your view in the Sound Off box below.

There are several examples that raise questions. France, finalists at the 2006 World Cup, are only 12th, while England, who did not even qualify for Euro 2008, are listed ninth.

France’s case is particularly striking. Les Bleus fell to their lowest ranking ever in April 1998, when they were placed 25th. Just three months later, they won the World Cup.

Mexico’s position in the rankings also puzzled many fans. Between 2001 and 2006, they were firmly inside the top 10 and at one stage climbed as high as fourth. That left many European supporters asking how such a placing could be justified.

During that time, Mexico were ranked above several teams widely regarded as European heavyweights, including Portugal. Yet Portugal reached the Euro 2004 final and then made it to the semi-finals of the 2006 World Cup in Germany.

Mexico and Portugal were even drawn in the same World Cup group, where Mexico finished second, five points behind Portugal. In the round of 16, Mexico were eliminated by an Argentina team that was talented but not without weaknesses.

Surely the World Cup, the biggest competition in football, should be the main measure of a team’s quality. Knockout tournaments do involve an element of fortune, but generally the strongest sides advance.

FIFA’s implication that Mexico were at one point the fourth-best national team in the world is difficult to accept. It is also hard to argue that they were superior to Portugal throughout that period when results on the field suggested the opposite.

As an alternative to FIFA’s rankings, which were introduced in 1993, football statisticians have created other rating systems.

FIFA changed its own method after the most recent World Cup, following criticism that rankings calculated over an eight-year span did not properly reflect a team’s current form.

“The increasingly high profile of the world ranking has also brought a certain amount of criticism that its calculation formula is too complicated. It was therefore decided in 2005 to revise the ranking in order to simplify the way in which it is calculated,” FIFA.com explained.

Before those changes, some rankings appeared even more surprising than they do now. Norway were ranked second twice during the 1990s, while the United States were placed fourth just two months before the 2006 World Cup.

At that tournament, the U.S. exited early after earning only one point and scoring two goals in three group matches, making their lofty ranking look highly questionable.

As of March 2009, Brazil and Argentina are the only teams from outside Europe in the top 10. Cameroon, in 16th place, are the highest-ranked African side. The United States are 17th, and Australia are the leading Asian nation in 32nd.

Whatever people think of the rankings, they are not going away. And Spain merit recognition for becoming only the sixth country, after Germany, Brazil, Italy, France and Argentina, to reach No. 1.

counterfactuals.output:
**Spain stays No. 1 in FIFA world rankings as debate over system continues**

Spain remained at the top of the FIFA world rankings in March 2009, holding its position as international football’s leading team after a dominant run that included its triumph at Euro 2008.

The European champion continued to lead the standings ahead of Germany and the Netherlands, with Italy, Brazil and Argentina also among the leading nations. Spain’s place at No. 1 reflected not only its tournament success but also its consistency in qualifying matches and friendlies over the previous several years.

Under the FIFA rankings system used at the time, teams earned points based on several factors: match results, the importance of the match, the strength of the opponent, the strength of the opposing confederation and the date of the match. More recent results carried greater weight, while older matches gradually declined in value over a four-year period.

That formula rewards teams for beating strong opponents in competitive matches. A World Cup qualifier, for example, is worth more than a friendly, and defeating a highly ranked team brings more points than beating a lower-ranked one.

Spain’s stay at No. 1 made sense to many observers. The team had gone unbeaten for a long stretch and was widely seen as the best side in the world, led by a golden generation featuring players such as Iker Casillas, Xavi, Andrés Iniesta, Fernando Torres and David Villa. Its possession-heavy style had reshaped expectations for international football and made Spain the team others were trying to catch.

Still, the rankings have long been a source of frustration for fans.

Critics argue that FIFA’s formula can produce results that feel disconnected from reality. Teams can rise or fall based on scheduling, the number of matches played, or the relative strength of their confederation. A nation that plays frequent competitive qualifiers may gain more ranking opportunities than one with fewer meaningful matches. Meanwhile, friendlies — even when used by coaches to experiment with lineups — can still affect a team’s position.

Fans also complain that the rankings can lag behind current form. Because results are calculated over several years, a team that was strong in a previous tournament cycle may remain highly ranked even after declining, while an improving side may take time to climb.

There is also the “eye test” problem: supporters often judge teams by recent performances, tournament pedigree and star power, while the rankings depend on a mathematical model. That means a team can appear too high or too low compared with public perception.

In March 2009, however, Spain’s ranking was difficult to dispute. The European champions were winning, playing stylish football and setting the standard for the rest of the world.

The controversy was less about Spain’s position than about the system itself — a reminder that while FIFA’s rankings provide a global snapshot, they rarely settle the debate over who is truly the best.

counterfactuals.output:
## Spain Stay Top — But FIFA’s Rankings Still Struggle to Pass the Eye Test

Spain’s ninth straight month at the top of FIFA’s world rankings should, in theory, be a statement of authority. A team holding the No. 1 position for that long ought to be the undisputed benchmark in international football: dominant, consistent and feared across continents.

Yet Spain’s continued reign also revives an old question: how much credibility should FIFA’s rankings really carry?

No one would argue Spain are undeserving of respect. Their technical quality remains exceptional, their player pool is deep, and their recent results have been strong enough to keep them ahead of the pack under FIFA’s points-based system. But the broader rankings table often feels less like a definitive hierarchy of world football and more like a mathematical compromise — one that can reward consistency, punish inactivity oddly, and occasionally produce placements that clash with common sense.

France are a useful example. On talent alone, they have a strong claim to being the world’s most formidable international side. Their squad depth is extraordinary, their tournament pedigree is recent and proven, and they have consistently operated at the sharp end of major competitions. If France are not No. 1, it is not because many would seriously argue they are inferior in a one-off match to every team above them. It is because the ranking formula does not simply measure who is “best” in the way supporters, coaches or players might understand it.

England raise a similar issue. They have been one of the most consistent tournament teams in recent years, regularly reaching the latter stages of major competitions. But their ranking position can fluctuate in ways that say as much about the opponents they face, the competitive weighting of matches and historical point accumulation as it does about their real strength. England may not have turned promise into a major men’s trophy, but few would deny they belong among the elite. The ranking system, however, can make the difference between second, fourth or sixth feel more scientific than it really is.

Then there are teams such as Mexico and the United States, whose positions have often sparked debate. Both benefit from being dominant or near-dominant forces in CONCACAF, where there are regular opportunities to collect ranking points. That is not to dismiss their quality — the USA in particular have produced an increasingly competitive generation, while Mexico remain one of the world’s most experienced international teams. But the rankings can sometimes flatter sides who win frequently within less demanding regional structures, while European and South American teams are more regularly forced into high-calibre contests.

Norway offer the opposite problem. On paper, any team featuring players of the calibre of Erling Haaland and Martin Ødegaard looks dangerous. But FIFA’s rankings are not designed to measure star power or theoretical potential; they measure results. Norway’s position has therefore often seemed low to those judging them by individual talent, yet arguably accurate when judged by tournament qualification and competitive consistency. In that sense, their case highlights both the strength and weakness of the system: it ignores hype, but it may also fail to capture how dangerous a side could be in the right circumstances.

The central flaw is that international football is not a league. Teams do not all play the same opponents, under the same conditions, with the same frequency or stakes. A ranking system tries to impose order on a chaotic calendar made up of qualifiers, friendlies, continental tournaments and the World Cup. Some confederations are more competitive than others. Some teams play more meaningful matches. Some benefit from regional dominance. Others are punished by brutal qualification routes.

FIFA has improved the methodology over the years, particularly by moving away from older systems that were more easily distorted. The current model, based partly on an Elo-style calculation, is more credible than previous versions. It accounts for opponent strength and match importance, which is sensible. But even a better formula cannot fully solve the structural imbalance of international football.

That is why Spain’s long stay at No. 1 should be treated as a headline, not a final verdict. They are unquestionably among the world’s best. They may even be the best. But the ranking itself does not prove it beyond debate.

Football rarely fits neatly into a spreadsheet. France may look stronger than their position. England may be judged more harshly by trophies than by consistency. Mexico and the USA may be lifted by regional realities. Norway may be dragged down by results despite possessing world-class talent. Spain may sit top for a ninth straight month and still not convince everyone they are the team to beat.

FIFA’s rankings are useful. They provide structure, seedings and a broad snapshot of form. But they should not be mistaken for absolute truth. In international football, credibility is still earned on the pitch — and no ranking table, however sophisticated, can fully replace that judgment.

The bigger question is whether their ranking will matter once the World Cup begins. Spain have often entered major tournaments with strong squads and high expectations, only to fall short. # Why Spain look worthy of FIFA’s No. 1 ranking — and why the rankings don’t always tell the whole story

In international football, the FIFA world ranking has long been treated as both a badge of honor and a source of debate. It can validate a team’s dominance, confuse fans with surprising placements and, at times, seem to reward consistency over genuine championship pedigree.

But Spain’s rise to No. 1 feels different.

This is not a team benefiting from a mathematical quirk or a soft run of fixtures. Spain’s claim is built on results, identity and a squad that has blended the country’s famous possession-based tradition with a sharper, faster and more ruthless edge.

After years of transition following the golden generation that won Euro 2008, the 2010 World Cup and Euro 2012, Spain have re-emerged as one of the most complete teams in world football. Their recent success has not been defined by sterile dominance of the ball, but by balance: control in midfield, vertical speed in attack and resilience against elite opposition.

Spain’s case for the top spot rests on one simple point: they have beaten the best, not merely avoided losing to them.

## A ranking backed by performances

FIFA’s rankings are not decided by public opinion or the aesthetic quality of a team’s football. They are calculated using results, the strength of opponents, the importance of matches and other weighting factors. That means major tournament games, knockout matches and victories over highly ranked teams carry significant value.

Spain have ticked those boxes.

Their recent tournament performances have shown a side capable of adapting to different types of opponents. Against teams that sit deep, Spain can still dominate territory and possession. Against stronger sides that press high, they now have the pace and directness to punish space behind the defense. And in tense knockout matches, they have shown an ability to manage pressure without abandoning their principles.

That versatility matters.

For much of the past decade, Spain were admired but also accused of being predictable. They could pass teams into exhaustion, but sometimes lacked the incision to turn control into clear chances. The current version looks more dangerous. The midfield remains technically gifted, but the attack has more width, more acceleration and more unpredictability.

In short, Spain are not just highly ranked because they win. They are highly ranked because their wins reflect a team with a convincing structure and a sustainable model.

## The return of Spanish authority

Spain’s previous era of dominance reshaped international football. The team led by Xavi, Andrés Iniesta, Sergio Busquets, Iker Casillas, David Villa and others turned possession into a form of defense and suffocated opponents through control.

This new Spain is not a carbon copy of that team — and that is part of its strength.

Modern international football is faster and more physically demanding. Pressing systems are more advanced. Transitions are more dangerous. Teams can no longer rely on possession alone to dominate. Spain have adjusted.

They still want the ball. They still value technical superiority. But they are now more willing to attack quickly, use wide players aggressively and create chaos when the moment calls for it.

That evolution helps explain why their No. 1 ranking feels earned rather than inflated. They have not simply revived an old formula; they have updated it.

## Why FIFA rankings can produce surprises

Still, history shows that FIFA’s rankings are not always a perfect reflection of who would be favored to win a World Cup or continental championship.

The system has produced some unusual headlines over the years. Mexico have been ranked inside the top four. Norway once climbed as high as No. 2. The United States were ranked No. 4 before the 2006 World Cup.

Each case became a reminder that FIFA’s ranking table is a measurement tool, not a universal truth.

It rewards results over a rolling period. It can benefit teams that perform consistently in qualifying or regional competitions. It can also be shaped by how often a nation plays, the relative strength of its confederation and the timing of victories and defeats.

That does not mean those teams were undeserving of respect. It means the rankings sometimes capture consistency better than elite-level danger.

## Mexico in the top four: consistency rewarded

Mexico’s climb into the upper tier of the rankings reflected a familiar pattern: strong regional performance, regular wins and competitive showings in major tournaments.

For years, Mexico were one of the most reliable teams outside Europe and South America. They routinely qualified for World Cups, performed well in Concacaf competitions and often proved difficult to beat on the global stage.

But being ranked among the world’s top four created an obvious debate. Were Mexico truly better than most of Europe’s and South America’s strongest teams? Or were they being rewarded for dominance and consistency within their competitive environment?

The answer was probably somewhere in between.

Mexico were a strong side, and their ranking was not random. But it also illustrated how FIFA’s formula could elevate teams that stacked up positive results, even if they were not widely viewed as serious World Cup favorites.

## Norway at No. 2: a product of results and timing

Norway’s rise to second in the FIFA rankings remains one of the most frequently cited anomalies.

In the 1990s, Norway were a formidable, disciplined and difficult opponent. They were not a glamorous team, but they were effective. They earned notable results, including against major football nations, and their direct, organized style made them awkward to play against.

Their high ranking was not simply a mistake. It reflected a period in which Norway were consistently producing good outcomes.

But few observers considered Norway the second-best team in the world in a broader, talent-based sense. Their position showed how rankings can reward efficiency and form while failing to capture depth, individual star power or tournament-winning potential.

It was a reminder that the FIFA table can be accurate according to its own formula while still feeling counterintuitive to the football public.

## The United States at No. 4 before the 2006 World Cup

Perhaps the most famous modern example came before the 2006 World Cup, when the United States entered the tournament ranked fourth in the world.

At the time, the US had become a consistent force in Concacaf. The team had reached the quarterfinals of the 2002 World Cup, performed well in regional competition and built a reputation for athleticism, organization and resilience.

On paper, the ranking reflected momentum.

But in Germany, the US struggled, finishing bottom of a difficult group that included Italy, Ghana and the Czech Republic. The result made the No. 4 ranking look inflated in hindsight.

The lesson was clear: rankings can capture what a team has done, but not always what is about to happen. They cannot fully account for stylistic matchups, tournament pressure, injuries, squad depth or the difference between regional dominance and global knockout-stage quality.

## Why Spain’s case is stronger

That is what separates Spain’s current No. 1 ranking from some of those historical curiosities.

Spain are not merely compiling wins in a less competitive region. They are doing it against Europe’s elite, in matches of consequence, with a squad that passes both the statistical and eye-test evaluations.

They have depth across the pitch. They have a recognizable tactical identity. They have players capable of controlling games and players capable of changing them. They have tournament credibility and recent evidence against top opposition.

There is also a difference between being highly ranked because others have stumbled and being highly ranked because a team has actively seized the position. Spain fall into the latter category.

Their football has been proactive, not accidental. Their rise has been built on more than avoiding defeats. It has been built on statement victories and a sense that the team’s ceiling is still rising.

## Rankings matter — but trophies matter more

The FIFA ranking will always invite debate because football resists neat measurement. A table can tell part of the story, but not all of it.

It cannot fully measure fear factor. It cannot quantify how a young winger changes the emotional temperature of a match. It cannot predict whether a goalkeeper will deliver in a penalty shootout or whether a midfield will hold under knockout pressure.

But it can reflect sustained excellence.

And in Spain’s case, the ranking aligns with what the football world has been watching: a national team that has rediscovered its authority, modernized its style and beaten top opponents when it mattered.

Past anomalies — Mexico in the top four, Norway at No. 2, the United States at No. 4 before the 2006 World Cup — show why rankings should be interpreted with caution. They are not destiny. They are not a trophy. They are not always a perfect hierarchy of football power.

But sometimes, the numbers and the reality meet.

Right now, Spain look like a team worthy of the summit.
